Reduce the series pair, find the charge, then the energy.
**Step 1 — combine the capacitors in series.**
1/C = 1/2 + 1/4
= 3/4
**C = 4/3 µF** ✓
less than either, as series capacitors must be.
**Step 2 — find the charge.**
Q = CV
= (4/3 x 10⁻⁶)(6)
= **8 x 10⁻⁶ C = 8 µC** ✓
and this same charge sits on **each** capacitor, since they are in series.
**Step 3 — find the energy.**
U = ½QV
= ½(8 x 10⁻⁶)(6)
= **24 x 10⁻⁶ J = 24 µJ** ✓
**A check by the other formula.**
U = ½CV² = ½(4/3 x 10⁻⁶)(36) = **24 µJ** ✓
**The voltage across each capacitor.**
2 µF: V = Q/C = 8/2 = **4 V**
4 µF: V = 8/4 = **2 V** ✓
total **6 V** ✓ as applied. The **smaller** capacitor takes the **larger** share, since
V = Q/C with Q common.
**Checking the energy capacitor by capacitor.**
2 µF: ½(8 µC)(4 V) = **16 µJ**
4 µF: ½(8 µC)(2 V) = **8 µJ**
total **24 µJ** ✓ consistent.
**Why series capacitors combine reciprocally.** Each carries the same charge but
contributes its own voltage drop, and the drops add ✓
V = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ = Q(1/C₁ + 1/C₂)
so 1/C_total is the sum of the reciprocals - the **opposite** of the resistor rule, which
is the usual place to slip.
**Reading the distractors.** **36 µC and 108 µJ** ✗ treat the capacitors as **parallel**,
giving 6 µF. **10 µC and 30 µJ** ✗ and **1 µC and 3 µJ** ✗ match no combination ✓ Note
that every option keeps U = ½QV consistent with its own Q, so the charge must be got
right first.
∴ 8 μC and 24 μJ.

The **smallest** effective capacitance comes from putting all three in **series**.
**Step 1 — recall which arrangement minimises C.** In **series** the reciprocals add, so
the total is **less than the smallest** member ✓ In **parallel** the capacitances add,
giving the **largest** possible value. Minimum therefore means all three in series.
**Step 2 — compute it.**
1/C = 1/1 + 1/2 + 1/4
= (4 + 2 + 1)/4
= 7/4
**C = 4/7 pF** ✓
**Step 3 — check the bound.** 4/7 = **0·571 pF**, which is indeed less than the smallest
capacitor, 1 pF ✓ as the series rule requires.
**The opposite extreme.** All three in **parallel** give
1 + 2 + 4 = **7 pF** ✓ the maximum obtainable - and note that 4/7 and 7 are reciprocally
related, which is a neat feature of this particular set.
**Why series capacitors reduce the total.** Connecting them in series is like increasing
the **plate separation** ✓ The same charge must be pushed through a longer effective
gap, so more voltage is needed per coulomb - that is, less capacitance.
**All the possible combinations, for completeness.**
all series: **0·571 pF** ✓ the minimum
1 in series with (2 ∥ 4): (1 x 6)/7 = **0·857 pF**
2 in series with (1 ∥ 4): (2 x 5)/7 = **1·43 pF**
4 in series with (1 ∥ 2): (4 x 3)/7 = **1·71 pF**
all parallel: **7 pF**
and various two-capacitor arrangements in between. The series combination is the
smallest of them all ✓
**The general rule to remember.** Capacitors behave **oppositely** to resistors ✓
series capacitors reduce like parallel resistors; parallel capacitors add like series
resistors. Mixing the two rules is the commonest error in this topic.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 pF** ✗ is the smallest single capacitor, but series
combination beats it. **2 pF** ✗ and **7/4 pF** ✗ are both larger still ✓ Any answer
of 1 pF or more cannot be the minimum, since the series value is necessarily below the
smallest member.
∴ 4/7 pF.

Gauss's law says the flux through a closed surface depends **only on the charge it
encloses**.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
Φ = **Q_enclosed/ε₀** ✓
Charges outside the surface contribute **nothing** to the net flux - their field lines
enter and leave again.
**Step 2 — read each surface from the figure.**
**S₁** encloses **−2Q and Q**, giving a net **−Q** ✓
**S₂** encloses **Q and −Q**, giving a net **zero** ✓
**S₃** encloses **all three**: −2Q + Q − Q = **−2Q** ✓
**Step 3 — convert to fluxes.**
through S₁: **−Q/ε₀** → matches **(ii)**
through S₂: **zero** → matches **(iii)**
through S₃: **−2Q/ε₀** → matches **(i)** ✓
**Step 4 — assemble the code.** a-ii, b-iii, c-i ✓
**Why external charges contribute nothing.** Every field line from an outside charge
that **enters** the closed surface must also **leave** it ✓ The inward and outward
contributions cancel exactly, so the **net** flux is unaffected - though the field at
each individual point certainly is.
**Why a negative flux.** A net **negative** enclosed charge means more field lines
**enter** the surface than leave it ✓ The sign of the flux follows the sign of the
enclosed charge.
**A check on S₂.** It holds equal and opposite charges, so every line leaving the +Q
ends on the −Q within the same surface ✓ Zero net flux, even though the field on the
surface is nowhere zero - a distinction worth keeping clear.
**Why the shape of the surface is irrelevant.** Gauss's law holds for **any** closed
surface, however irregular ✓ Only the enclosed charge matters, which is what makes the
law so powerful.
**The caution about using it to find E.** Zero flux does **not** mean zero field ✓ To
extract E from Gauss's law one needs enough **symmetry** - spherical, cylindrical or
planar - for E to be constant over the surface. Here the law gives the flux, and the
flux alone.
∴ a − ii, b − iii, c − i.

Write g in terms of G and rearrange.
**Step 1 — state the acceleration due to gravity at the surface.**
g = **GM/R²** ✓
**Step 2 — form the required ratio.**
g/G = **M/R²** ✓
**Checking the dimensions.**
[M/R²] = kg m⁻² ✓
and directly, [g]/[G] = (m s⁻²)/(N m² kg⁻²) = (m s⁻²)(kg² )/(kg m s⁻² x m²) = **kg
m⁻²** ✓ the two agree.
**Why the ratio is useful.** It isolates the quantities belonging to the **planet**
alone ✓ G is a universal constant, the same everywhere in the universe; M and R are
properties of the Earth. The ratio g/G therefore measures "how much planet" there is
per unit area.
**The numerical value for the Earth.**
M = 5·97 x 10²⁴ kg, R = 6·37 x 10⁶ m
M/R² = 5·97 x 10²⁴/(4·06 x 10¹³) = **1·47 x 10¹¹ kg m⁻²**
and g/G = 9·81/(6·67 x 10⁻¹¹) = **1·47 x 10¹¹** ✓ identical.
**How the Earth's mass was first found.** Not by weighing it, but from exactly this
relation ✓ g and R were known by 1700; once **Cavendish** measured G in 1798 with his
torsion balance, M = gR²/G followed at once. His experiment was justly described as
"weighing the Earth".
**How g varies between planets.** Through M/R² ✓
the **Moon**: M is 1/81 of Earth's and R is 1/3·7, giving g = **1·6 m s⁻²**
**Jupiter**: much more massive but also much larger, giving **24·8 m s⁻²**
It is the **ratio**, not the mass alone, that decides.
**Reading the distractors.** **R²/M** ✗ is the reciprocal. **MR²** ✗ and **M/R** ✗ do
not follow from g = GM/R² ✓ A dimensional check settles each in one line.
∴ M/R².

Kepler's third law relates the period to the orbital radius as **T² ∝ R³**.
**Step 1 — state the law.**
T² = (4π²/GM) R³ ✓
so, for the same planet, **T ∝ R^(3/2)**.
**Step 2 — write the ratio.**
T₂/T₁ = (R₂/R₁)^(3/2)
= (3R/R)^(3/2)
= **3^(3/2) = 3√3 = √27** ✓
**Step 3 — find the new period.**
T₂ = 4 x √27
= **4√27 hours** ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate it.**
√27 = 5·196, so T₂ ≈ **20·8 hours** ✓
Tripling the radius multiplies the period by about five.
**Where the law comes from.** Equating the gravitational force to the centripetal
requirement:
GMm/R² = mω²R, with ω = 2π/T
GM/R² = 4π²R/T²
**T² = 4π²R³/(GM)** ✓
**Why the satellite's own mass does not appear.** It cancels from both sides ✓ All
satellites at the same radius have the same period, whatever their mass - which is why
a space station and a loose bolt stay together in orbit.
**The orbital speed, for contrast.**
v = √(GM/R), so **v ∝ 1/√R** ✓ The outer satellite is **slower** as well as having
further to go, and both effects lengthen its period.
**A familiar check.** Earth's period about the Sun is 1 year at 1 AU; Mars orbits at
1·52 AU:
T = 1·52^(3/2) = **1·87 years** ✓ the observed value.
**Reading the distractors.** **16 hours** ✗ would be T ∝ R², too steep. **4 hours** ✗
assumes no change at all. **4√8 ≈ 11·3** ✗ would correspond to a doubling of the radius,
since 2^(3/2) = √8 ✓ That last option is a well-aimed trap for anyone who misreads
3R as 2R.
∴ 4√27.

Rearrange Newton's law of gravitation for G and read off the dimensions.
**Step 1 — start from the force law.**
F = Gm₁m₂/r²
so
**G = Fr²/(m₁m₂)** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute the dimensions.**
[G] = [M L T⁻²][L²]/[M²]
= [M L³ T⁻²]/[M²]
= **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]** ✓
**Step 3 — check against the SI unit.** G is measured in **N m² kg⁻²**:
(kg m s⁻²)(m²)/(kg²) = **kg⁻¹ m³ s⁻²** ✓ exactly the same.
**The numerical value.**
G = **6·674 x 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²** ✓ the smallest and least precisely known of the
fundamental constants - gravity is extraordinarily feeble, and shielding an experiment
from stray masses is very hard.
**A second route, through g.** From g = GM/R²:
[G] = [L T⁻²][L²]/[M] = **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]** ✓ the same, as it must be.
**Why the power of M is negative.** G appears in the **denominator** of the mass
dependence when the equation is rearranged ✓ A larger G would mean stronger gravity for
the same masses, so G must carry M⁻¹ to balance the two masses in the numerator of the
force law.
**A use for the dimensions.** The combination
√(ℏG/c³) = **1·6 x 10⁻³⁵ m**
is the **Planck length**, built from G, ℏ and c alone ✓ Such combinations are possible
only because G's dimensions are known.
**Reading the distractors.** **M⁻¹L²T⁻²** ✗ has one power of length too few - it omits
the r² from the force law. **M⁰L⁰T⁰** ✗ would make G dimensionless, like a refractive
index. **M⁻¹L³T⁻¹** ✗ has the wrong power of time ✓ Checking against the familiar unit
N m² kg⁻² is the quickest test of any candidate.
∴ M⁻¹L³T⁻².
